items.question: How do you understand Silicon Valley’s heavy investment in robotics?
items.object: Silicon Valley’s investment in robotics
items.answer: I think everyone in Silicon Valley sees robotics as perhaps one of the most important transformations about to happen, so every company is investing heavily to assemble its robotics teams and build large models for robots. And recently, if you look at the first generation of Gemini Robotics—the version from March—there may already have been 120 people on the author list; this time perhaps 160 to 180 people.

items.question: What drew you from physics-based character animation into robotics?
items.object: The transition from physics-based character animation to robotics
items.answer: My PhD was in graphics. At that time I also interned at Pixar. What I had always worked on was called animation. There are many approaches to animation. At Pixar, Pixar had many principles it insisted on—for example, it never uses motion-capture systems; it believes everything should be hand-tuned. But if you research animation, it isn’t about hand-tuning those animations; it is about using mathematical and physical methods to see whether, in a simulated environment, you can make, for example, a human form or an animal form walk naturally. What I did then was called physics-based character animation. As I kept doing it, I felt there were many AI components in it—I increasingly used AI to solve these problems. This was probably in my third or fourth year. Then I felt it was too similar to robotics, and I also felt I didn’t want my work to be only for entertainment, for games and film and television. So I told my advisor I wanted to try robotics. I wanted to use graphics methods to transform the entire robotics industry.

items.question: How do you understand the skepticism you encountered in 2015 toward your ambition to transform robotics with graphics methods?
items.object: Transforming robotics with graphics methods
items.answer: I wanted a faculty job, and at the time I received interviews from many very good schools, such as Cornell. But I said then that I wanted to transform robotics with graphics methods. I think people were very skeptical at the time, because I was just entering this field and the vast majority of my background was in graphics. So I did not get the faculty job I wanted. I went to work in Silicon Valley instead—first at a startup, then at Google.

items.question: Why did you see computer graphics as a promising way to transform robotics?
items.object: Computer graphics as a way to transform robotics
items.answer: Let me give a few examples. In graphics, people may know there is a very famous Berkeley professor named Sergey Levine. He also used to do graphics. At SIGGRAPH presentations, he and I were often one after the other—perhaps I would present first, then he would. Yet we both independently switched to robotics, which shows the two fields are very closely related. At that time, I felt robotics was still very rule-based. People used traditional control methods; for example, there was a method called MPC, model predictive control. People build physical models and then use optimization algorithms to calculate, for example, motion trajectories. There are many difficulties in that. I often tell people that in the past, to do robotics, you definitely needed a PhD; otherwise you could not even make sense of the mathematics. But graphics has many AI algorithms in it. This was simple at the time because everything was in the computer, in simulation, so you could obtain every piece of information you needed about the robot—joints, forces, all kinds of things. So you could use AI methods to solve all kinds of control problems. At the time, I felt simulation and the real world were basically similar things, so if something could work in simulation, it should also work in the real world. Robotics was still very dumb at the time. There was a DARPA Robotics Challenge, where many humanoid robots did relatively simple things, such as going over a slope, driving a car, or turning a valve. The robots fell down and so on; they looked very dumb. But in graphics—in simulation—robots could do somersaults, run, and do everything. So I felt the gap between the two sides was very obvious. If we could bring what worked in simulation into the real world, robots would make enormous progress. That is why I felt I would transform robotics with graphics technology.

items.question: How do you assess the impact of your first Google paper, “Sim2Real: Learning Agile Locomotion for Quadruped Robots,” on robotics?
items.object: “Sim2Real: Learning Agile Locomotion for Quadruped Robots” and its impact on robotics
items.answer: My first paper at Google was called “Sim2Real: Learning Agile Locomotion for Quadruped Robots.” Sim2Real means going from simulation to the real world. And the method I used was entirely deep reinforcement learning, which was relatively new even in graphics, and nobody was using it in robotics at all. After that first paper came out, it received a lot of praise. I think it was the first—how should I put it—paradigm shift in the past decade: using reinforcement learning to solve walking and gait problems. Let me describe it. Maybe ten years ago, people thought the best robots were Boston Dynamics robots: its dog was called Spot, and its humanoid was called Atlas. They could do parkour—very impressive. But the entire academic community did not know how they did it. Only recently did people learn that they used MPC, but pushed it to the limit. Yet perhaps five years later, you saw that everyone could run and jump, box and dance. For example, this year you see Unitree and so on; they can box and dance, and recently all kinds can climb walls and do somersaults. This is actually because everyone adopted the same technologies: reinforcement learning and Sim2Real. Personally, I think my initial paper pioneered the entire application of reinforcement learning and Sim2Real to quadruped robots. Looking back now, that paper—or computer graphics—really and thoroughly changed robotics development over the past five to ten years.

items.question: How do you place your use of reinforcement learning in robotics in relation to the rise of large language models?
items.object: Reinforcement learning and large language models as paradigm shifts in robotics
items.answer: The rise of large language models was perhaps in the past five years. Reinforcement learning—that was eight years ago, in 2018, seven or eight years ago. But I think the first paradigm shift in the past decade was definitely reinforcement learning; the second paradigm shift was large language models.

items.question: What do you see as the most important changes large language models have brought to robotics?
items.object: The impact of large language models on robotics
items.answer: Before large language models came out, many robots were still dealing with low-level control—how to walk well, and how to do path planning so your hand could, for example, grasp this bottle without bumping into anything. But robots had no common sense, and they did not understand language. So if you wanted a robot to do something, you had to program it before it could do it. But once you had large language models, first, they understood human language. So you could directly use natural language to talk to it and tell it to do things. That was an important breakthrough: anyone could direct a robot to do things. That is the first thing. The second thing is common sense. Previously people felt robots were so hard—not only because of the control problem, but because robots had no common sense. For example, “make me a cup of coffee” is a very simple instruction, but it had no idea what it meant or what steps could make a cup of coffee. But if you ask Gemini or ChatGPT what steps are needed to make a cup of coffee, it will list them step by step. If you ask for more detailed steps, it can give you a very detailed plan. So when you use a large language model to control a robot, the robot has common sense. It can understand what concrete steps are needed to do something. Previously, robots had no brain. After large language models, you can think of them as having a brain and cognition, enabling them to do many complex things.

items.object: The complementary roles of reinforcement learning and large language models in robotics
items.answer: I think it is a little like the cerebrum and cerebellum. The cerebrum is thought—reasoning and planning. So large language models are more like the cerebrum. So you may need both the cerebrum and cerebellum.

items.question: How do you view the claim that robotics foundation models should be an independent discipline rather than an extension of multimodal large models?
items.object: The independence of robotics foundation models from multimodal large models
items.answer: I don’t think there is a right or wrong answer. People have different biases. From my perspective, I have to acknowledge that the development of robot intelligence over the past several years has mainly relied on multimodal large models, so it is not just language models. It is a multimodal model. But what do multimodal models lack? They lack robot-action output. A multimodal model can take in images and language, and its output may be text. But it cannot output controls for a robot. So what we often do is use a large language model as a base model and add robot-action data, so it can output robot actions and control robots. From my perspective, much of my work is still about how to complete current multimodal models so they can output robot actions and control robots. Is it a completely independent discipline? So far, not yet. In the future, perhaps when you encounter various bottlenecks, need different data formats, or need a more complete world model, it may become a more independent discipline. But now, I think the overwhelming majority working on VLAs and robot large models are still doing some kind of fine-tuning on large language models or multimodal language models.

items.question: How close do you think general-purpose robots are to being useful in everyday life?
items.object: The readiness of general-purpose robots for real-world use
items.answer: If you are doing one task or a series of very similar tasks, it can now do quite well. But if you want true generalization—real generalization capability—if you want a humanoid robot that can do many things, we are still very far away. Even models such as Gemini Robotics, which emphasize generalization heavily, can do many things: you can tell them in natural language to open this bottle cap, organize this bag, and so on. But their success rate is still not very high. For very simple pick and place—grasping something and putting it somewhere—the success rate may be over 90 percent, even 100 percent. But for many things that require fine manipulation, such as pulling up a zipper, it is very difficult. You have to grasp the right place and pull in a particular direction. For things like that, the success rate may be 30 or 40 percent. A 30 or 40 percent success rate is unusable in real life. So although our progress is very fast, our gap is also very large. I think it will still take several years for robots to become mature enough to enter all walks of life and help us.

items.question: Why do you think taking five to ten years to move from a robotics demo to real deployment is reasonable?
items.object: The timeline from a robotics research prototype to real deployment
items.answer: Generally, in research, you have an idea. Then going from an idea to a prototype is fast, because once you make a prototype, you can write a paper. That cycle might be six months, at most a year. Once you have written a paper, before you have the confidence to bring it out for a live demo rather than merely record a video, it may take one or two years. When writing a paper, you make many assumptions, so it may only work within a very narrow range. Then from beginning to do live demos to truly deploying it may take five to ten years. Consider autonomous driving. From the beginning—for example, saying at the DARPA Robotics Challenge that I can drive twenty-plus kilometers well—to later, when every vendor could say it could do a demo in a fixed campus, to perhaps today—we could count it as deployed, since Waymo and Tesla both have their own products—there was indeed a ten-year gap. So I don't think ten years from a demo to real deployment is particularly exaggerated.

items.question: How do you think about pursuing general-purpose humanoid robots versus building specialized robots for one domain at a time?

items.answer: I don’t think there is right or wrong, but the world’s development is not about right or wrong, and the two paths are equally possible. What may happen in the end is that there will be a big figure—perhaps Elon Musk, perhaps Steve Jobs—a visionary person who instills the idea that humanoid robots and general-purpose robots are the ultimate solution. Once a big figure speaks, many followers will come, a lot of money will come in, and a lot of talent will come in, ultimately making that path the one that truly gets solved. So I am not saying it is wrong to make specialized robots and solve one domain at a time. One model might translate English to Chinese, and another might do some other QA. But later people found that once you genuinely have a generalist model, specialist models simply cannot compete with it. That is another example of why people believe more in general robots.

items.question: Why do you see data as a fundamental bottleneck in robotics development?
items.object: Data as a bottleneck in robotics development
items.answer: I think one of the biggest problems is still data. For language models, data is free. items.question: How do you think about the different kinds of data needed to train robots?
items.object: The data pyramid in robotics
items.answer: You need lots and lots of very different data. In robotics, people often discuss a data pyramid. The pyramid works like this. At the very bottom are highly scalable, massive amounts of data. This may be data available on the internet. The next layer may be video data, possibly what we call egocentric video data—data of doing things as seen from a person’s perspective. There is a great deal of this kind of data on YouTube. It is easy to collect, because when you do something you may only need to wear glasses or a camera, so its volume is large. But humans and robots have very different morphologies, so this data is not especially useful, or at least people do not yet know how to use it. Above that may be simulation data. This data is closer to a robot’s morphology and includes lots of robot-action labels, but there is a sim-to-real gap: data in simulation and real-world physics are ultimately different; simulation is only a mathematical simplification. Above that may be robot-specific data: robot data obtained through teleoperation or other means. I think you need every level of data, but in different quantities; collecting data at different levels has different costs; and all of these data are important.

items.question: What do you see as the significance of adding thinking traces to the robot model in Gemini Robotics 1.5?
items.object: Thinking traces in Gemini Robotics 1.5
items.answer: I think that is a relatively important breakthrough. Previously, a VOA model took images as input, along with language expressing what the task was, and output motor angles—for direct robot control. Now we also make what is called a thinking trace—how the robot is thinking—an output. So if I want to do a task, such as sorting clothes by color, the robot first has to think. The task is actually quite complex: it has to think that this is red and should go into the red pile, while this garment is white and should go into the white pile. There are many very small steps. The previous generation of robot models could not think through things in such detail or do such a multi-step task. This generation can think: what color is this, and if I know that, what should I do next? So it first outputs some text to think about how to solve the problem, then, based on that text, outputs a set of actions and does it. Next it continues outputting text to think about the next step, then outputs actions again. This lets a very complex task that requires many steps be decomposed. So now it can do very difficult tasks. The second benefit is that the robot can tell people what it wants to do next and why it wants to do it, adding much more transparency to human-robot interaction. Whether from the safety perspective or the human-robot interaction perspective, this at least makes people feel more at ease, because they know how the robot is thinking.

items.question: How do you see Motion Transfer in Gemini Robotics 1.5 addressing the scarcity of robot training data?
items.object: Cross-embodiment data sharing through Motion Transfer in Gemini Robotics 1.5
items.answer: In particular, data collected using robot A can only teach the tasks and skills on robot A. If robot A is upgraded—perhaps its camera is replaced, mounted in a different position, or its arm has an additional degree of freedom—then all previously collected data is useless. And other robots, such as humanoid robots, robot B, and robot C, have different configurations, so their data cannot be pooled and used interchangeably. This leaves even less data, because you have to collect it separately for every individual robot. With Gemini Robotics 1.5, we found that regardless of which robot you use—at least for the three we tested: ALOHA, a very simple bimanual robot; Bi-Arm Franka, a more industrial-grade, more powerful robot; and Apptronik’s humanoid robot—when we put all the data together and developed a new technique called Motion Transfer, it could better use cross-embodiment data so that a task seen on robot A could also be performed by robot B. For example, suppose you learned to drive. I have never learned the task of driving, but I also learn to drive.

items.question: How do you think Gemini 1.5’s division into fast and slow models addresses the limits of reasoning in VOA?
items.object: The limits of VOA reasoning and Gemini 1.5’s fast-and-slow model division
items.answer: The thinking we currently have in VOA is still relatively weak thinking, because, as I said, it has many constraints. I find that generally, if a task only requires decomposition into a few steps—for example, if I want to sort fruit by color or sort clothes by color, the first step may be identifying the color, the second recognizing which of the other piles corresponds to that color, and the third placing it in the corresponding pile. This kind of relatively simple reasoning is possible. But if it needs to obtain additional information, it cannot do that. For example, if I say, “Help me pack my luggage,” it might say, “To pack luggage, I want to know where you are traveling, how long you will be there, and what the weather will be like.” It needs to obtain more information and think through all of it. That cannot be done on the VOA side. So in Gemini 1.5, we made a fast-and-slow model division: there is a relatively slow model that can do this very long thinking and make decisions. For example, for “help me pack my luggage,” it can search Google Search, your calendar, and weather reports; think for twenty seconds; come up with a plan; and ask whether the plan is reasonable. Then on the VOA side, when it executes that plan, it can say, “I may need to put this pile of clothes in,” and take them one by one.

items.object: Overfitting when adding thinking to a model
items.answer: One possibility is overfitting. When you add thinking, you need to annotate how many tasks should be thought through. Before training, you collect lots of data. When collecting it, you have to say, “This is how I thought; this is what I will do next; and this is my action.” But if those annotations are very uniform, overfitting can easily occur, meaning that its thinking only makes sense when doing these particular things. If it does other unseen tasks, because it has not seen them, its thinking can indeed become very strange and it can do things that make no sense at all.

items.question: Why do you see the transfer of vertical tasks from Bi-arm Franka to ALOHA as a qualitative change in cross-embodiment learning?
items.object: Cross-embodiment learning and the transfer of vertical tasks from Bi-arm Franka to ALOHA
items.answer:
The first time I saw this result, it left a very deep impression on me, because I felt this was genuinely a qualitative change. People have talked about cross-embodiment for many years, but I think this concept has been somewhat oversold. Even early on, Google itself published a paper called RTX, working with perhaps more than twenty different universities and labs to collect different robot datasets, mix them together, train a large model, and say that combining data from those more than twenty schools brought advantages or benefits. But it was difficult to quantify. More recently, with Physical Intelligence and many robot large models, they all say they have different embodiments, mix their data together, and thereby make the system more general, but that too is difficult to quantify.

This time, we found that ALOHA is a tabletop robot, so everything it does is on a tabletop. All our data collection may be things such as grasping something on the table and putting it elsewhere, opening a bottle cap on the table, or writing. It has never seen 3D scenes. It has never seen, for example, a vertical plane or a cabinet with different heights, where it can do many things. So if you give it an output with different heights and say, “Get me the book on the upper shelf,” it cannot do it, because that is completely outside its training dataset. What it will do is still fumble around touching things on the tabletop, even though the bookshelf is vertical. But we have another robot called Bi-arm Franka, for which much of the data collection is in a vertical setting. It has many tools that it can take down vertically from something called a workbench. Then we train with the data together. ALOHA has never seen this vertical scene. But when you put what Franka can do into ALOHA’s setting, ALOHA suddenly can do that kind of thing too.

items.question: How do you understand the scope of generalization achieved by motion transfer across robots?
items.object: Task-level versus robot-embodiment-level generalization in motion transfer
items.answer: First, it does not mean that if you now give me a new robot, it can do those things without any training. That is not what it means. It means that among robots for which I have training data, even though I have not seen this particular task, someone else has seen this task. Then I can do that task. So it has some generalizability, but its generalization is at the task level, not at the robot-embodiment level.

items.question: How do you view the claim that embodied intelligence lacks clear, verifiable feedback signals?
items.object: Feedback signals in embodied intelligence
items.answer: I do not really understand what “feedback” means here. I think when you have data and use traditional methods such as imitation learning, you already have sufficient signals. I do not understand what it means to say that it lacks signals. But if you mean reinforcement learning, it needs a signal called a reward. Many tasks make it hard to write a reward function. For example, if I want to put this plate of food in the refrigerator, how do I express success or failure mathematically? It is difficult to express that reward function. I agree with that. I think this has to be explained differently in different situations. For imitation learning, I do not think signals are a problem. But for reinforcement learning, how to specify a task using a reward function is indeed a difficult and unresolved problem.

items.question: Why do you think specifying rewards remains such a difficult problem for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation?
items.object: Reward specification for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation
items.answer: I do not think this problem has been solved well. To digress briefly, why did reinforcement learning solve the walking problem for quadruped robots? Because the reward function is particularly easy—not especially easy, but relatively straightforward. You only need to move forward and not fall down, so you can easily write a mathematical expression. But for manipulation, there are too many different tasks. For example, I want to pick up a chopstick. It is actually difficult to express mathematically whether I picked up the chopstick. For example, if I want to put something into a drawer, it is difficult to write a mathematical expression for whether the thing is in the drawer. There are thousands upon thousands of such different tasks, and you would need reward signals to tune all of them. I think that is almost impossible. That is why reinforcement learning has not been solved very well in manipulation: this reward function is very difficult to specify.

items.question: Why do you see imitation learning as providing sufficient training signals for your cross-morphology transfer tasks?

items.answer: We currently mainly do imitation learning. We are not doing it through reinforcement learning. Since imitation has a demonstration, it has labels. You have an example to imitate. You only need to make your neural network’s output as close as possible to the labels, and there is no problem.

items.question: What do you think determines how effective learning transfer between different robot embodiments can be?
items.object: Transfer of robot learning across different embodiments
items.answer: Although we have many examples proving the transfer succeeds, we also have many examples showing that in many situations the transfer is not very successful. I think how different the morphologies of two robots are has a big impact. For example, transferring from a single-arm gripper robot to a bimanual humanoid robot is certainly a very, very difficult problem. The three robots we use are all bimanual. Although their configurations differ substantially—some have six degrees of freedom, some seven, and some more—they are all bimanual. Going from a gripper to, for example, a dexterous hand, a physical dexterous hand, would certainly be more difficult than gripper-to-gripper transfer. There is also something called the embodiment gap. If that embodiment gap is very large, transfer across configurations becomes relatively difficult. That is one point. Second, we find that the volume of data collected for different embodiments is also very important. If you have already collected a huge amount of data, you may already do the task very well without transfer from other embodiments. The positive delta from other embodiments will be very small. But if, for example, it is difficult to collect data for humanoid robots, while you have a very large amount of data on ALOHA, then the transfer can be very effective.

items.question: How do you see tool use expanding a robot’s capabilities as a physical AI agent?
items.object: Tool use in physical AI agents
items.answer: First, a robot is a physical agent. I think the definition of an agent is that it can make decisions and execute actions. This article emphasizes one important agent feature: it can use tools. Our embodied reasoning model can write code and look up websites, for example. It can use these tools to make decisions. We have several videos where, for example, you ask it to collect or sort garbage. Depending on the location, it can say, “I’m in San Francisco,” search Google Maps to find your location, and then follow local laws and regulations. It can decide how garbage should be sorted. These are examples of using digital tools. They enable robots to do web searches, greatly broadening their knowledge base. Rather than relying only on the large model having captured common sense, web search and these other tools greatly expand a robot’s functionality and capability.

items.question: Why do you see scalable training data as a particularly important direction for robotics beyond Gemini Robotics 1.5?
items.object: Scalable data sources for training robotics models beyond Gemini Robotics 1.5
items.answer: There are many, many possible directions. We also discussed some future directions in the final chapter. One point we value particularly is data. As I have emphasized many times: data, data, data. Teleoperation is still very difficult data to obtain. Finding ways to use less and less teleoperation data and more data that can be obtained quickly to train such large models may be a very important step. So we will devote more effort to, for example, using simulation data. Using human video data from YouTube, and even data generated by current models, such as video-generation data. Because this kind of data can be obtained in large quantities, I think it is a more economical and effective way to obtain robot data. items.question: How do you see the relationship between the research paradigms of robotics foundation models and large language models?
items.object: Research paradigms of robotics foundation models and large language models
items.answer: I think they are still very different. As I said, they are not really two independent disciplines; rather, A is making use of B. So, for example, with large language models, there is a lot around how to train multimodality, what pre-training should look like, what post-training should look like, how R-RL should be used. But robotics' current application of these large language models is more about adding more data and adding new outputs on top of an existing large language model. So the approaches are still very different. For example, very few companies truly pre-train a robotics large model from scratch.

items.question: Why do you see robotics foundation-model research as following a different paradigm from large language-model research?
items.object: The relationship between robotics foundation-model research and large language-model research
items.answer: Because of cost and data. Pre-training a large model is extremely expensive; you may need tens of thousands of GPUs, or several months of time. And at the same time, you do not have that much robotics data. So basically, because of data limitations and the cost of pre-training large models, people generally add robotics data to an already pre-trained large model and fine-tune it. That makes the overall paradigm very different. So I think the two sides do have things they can learn from each other, but they are not two parallel disciplines where everything maps one-to-one and can be mutually borrowed.

items.question: How do you understand the changing meaning of simulation with the rise of video generation models such as Veo and Sora 2?
items.object: The changing meaning of simulation with video generation models
items.answer: I would describe the change this way: in the past, simulation referred to physical simulation. So what people called simulation might be Bullet, MuJoCo, Isaac Gym—these were called simulation. It was essentially solving physical equations on a computer and calculating motion trajectories. That was simulation in the past. But now, with the rise of video generation models such as Veo and Sora 2, many people think simulation can simply mean generating a video. If the video appears physically correct, it is also a new kind of simulation in that sense.

items.question: What value do you see in using video generation to create scenes compared with traditional simulation?
items.object: Video generation as a way to create simulation scenes
items.answer: It actually solves many problems. For example, if I want to generate arbitrary scenes, in traditional simulation you need someone to model them. After modeling, it is like making a game: you need many designers to assemble all the scenes and all the assets. And if I want 500 household scenes, you have to build them one by one by hand. That is very difficult. But if I want videos of 500 household scenes, I just need 500 different prompts. One person can say, I want a pink bed plus two rattan cabinets; another can say, I have a very large, white bed. With just different language inputs, you can instantly generate two completely different videos or simulations. But in traditional simulation, you had to manually construct each scene one by one.

items.question: Why would you hesitate to call current video generation models world models?
items.object: Video generation models as world models
items.answer: The definition of a world model is: if you provide the previous frame and provide the robot's action, you can predict the next frame. Right now, all video generation models—most of them—do not let you change the outcome of the next frame by inputting a robot action or a human action. So I would not call them world models yet. items.question: Why do you see defining data quality as a research problem for robotics and the emerging data foundry industry?

items.answer: Data quality is still extremely important. If the data quality is very poor, then more data may produce worse results. items.question: How has your experience combining traditional control theory with reinforcement learning shaped your view of hierarchical versus end-to-end unified models in robotics?
items.object: Hierarchical versus end-to-end unified models in robotics
items.answer: Let me share another story. Although I said my first paper at Google was on reinforcement learning, I personally did not especially believe in it. Although that paper had a very strong so-called sign of life, suggesting it might work, you also encounter—and I encountered—many difficulties: how do you tune the reward function? And if training results are bad, PPO was very inefficient at that time. So I wondered whether there was some shortcut. I thought, why not combine traditional control theory with reinforcement learning? At the lower level I would still use traditional control theory, but use reinforcement learning to tune some parameters. Our team worked on that direction for quite a while, and the results were good, because the effect was immediate: the lower-level parts already more or less worked, and reinforcement learning could immediately make them work. But the trajectory of history did not move in the direction I imagined. Instead, people did completely end-to-end reinforcement learning—state in, action out—and after a few years that indeed became mainstream. I think that sometimes, to solve practical problems, or because you think you can get better results in the short term, you take some shortcuts. You make some of these hierarchical models. But at least my past experience tells me that perhaps if you invest directly in the end-to-end large model or unified large model you ultimately believe in, that may win in the end.

items.question: How has your understanding of the need for tactile sensing in robots changed as robotic hardware has developed?
items.object: The importance of tactile sensing as robotic hardware develops
items.answer: I think robotics development definitely needs more modalities. Here is a small story about my own journey. People have always said that tactile sensing—touch—is very important. I always believed that too, because intuitively, you have skin every day and feel the world you touch. Then at Stanford there was a paper called ALOHA. It was the first time I saw that people could use vision—entirely vision—to teleoperate an ALOHA robot to do very complex things, including taking a credit card, a very thin object, out of a handbag. I had thought that only touch could achieve something like that. But the appearance of ALOHA really slapped me in the face. I realized that many things could also be solved through vision. So I held that belief for a while—that perhaps vision was enough. Or vision could do 95 percent of things, and perhaps only the remaining 5 percent needed touch. Until recently, dexterous hands began becoming more and more common, and I went to some places and used teleoperation to control dexterous hands. One example was using scissors with a dexterous hand. Using scissors is a very simple thing: you put your hand through the two loops, then you can use the scissors. But at that time there was no tactile feedback. Completely through vision, I put my hand—the hand in front of the machine that controlled the dexterous hand—through the two loops of the scissors, and then opened and closed my hand on my side. But because I had no touch, I did not know when to open and when to close. Since the two loops were very large, when you open and close at an inappropriate time, your hand merely moves inside those two loops and does not control the opening and closing of the scissors at all. So that made me realize that touch is very important when you have a dexterous hand. The reason I previously thought touch was unimportant was actually a limitation of the hardware at the time. If you only have a gripper, then you can see from afar that my gripper is opening and closing. Then I can make very good judgments. But when you have a dexterous hand, five fingers, and need to perform very complex behaviors and tasks, touch feels indispensable.

items.question: How do you think about the choice between pursuing the final model for robotics and working toward near-term deployment?
items.object: Robotics research strategies focused on the final model versus near-term deployment
items.answer: There is actually a lot to discuss there. It completely depends on whether you are doing things at a big company or doing a startup. It may also depend on whether you are working in Silicon Valley or in China on similar problems, because I think everyone's goals are different. Personally, what I tend to do is solve AI in the physical world. So I focus very strongly on what the final form looks like and what the final model looks like; everything else may just be a distraction. But if you are a startup, and capital expects you to survive or be profitable, then it is hard to say that you will put everything else aside and not make money, just to build the final model for 20 years from now. So you may think about achieving some near-term deployment, getting the data flywheel turning, and gradually solving the problem. An analogy, though I do not know whether it is entirely appropriate, is that Waymo and Tesla have adopted very different strategies. Both want to solve autonomous driving. Waymo looked at the endpoint: I want L4. I want truly driverless operation, no matter where it is, without a person; I do not even want a steering wheel. So many of its decisions were about how to get to L4. Tesla said we are not in a hurry; we sell cars anyway, so we can go little by little from L2 and L2.5 upward, get the data flywheel turning, and eventually may also reach L4. So I think neither path is right or wrong. I am not saying everyone must do end-to-end or must do humanoids. They may arrive at the same destination by different routes, solving the same problem in different ways.

items.question: How did the growing accessibility of reinforcement learning shape your view of robot-locomotion research?
items.object: The growing accessibility of reinforcement learning for robot locomotion
items.answer: After doing reinforcement learning, I spent a long time doing gaits and locomotion and related things. I worked on quadrupeds, and then reached a point where I felt that field had become extremely crowded. With reinforcement learning, it is not hard to use; it is actually very easy to use. Let me make another aside: broadly speaking, when a technology becomes easier and easier to use, it spreads quickly. Take gait control: for a humanoid robot to walk, at the beginning, as I said, people used MPC, model predictive control. At that time, you needed a PhD to really understand the mathematics and solve the equations, so that algorithm or technology was still far from being widespread. After that came reinforcement learning. With reinforcement learning, I think many high-school students today can download a reinforcement-learning package online, such as PPO, get something like Isaac Gym from NVIDIA, put them together, train and deploy. Many high-school students can probably do that. That means it will quickly become extremely crowded, because many people can enter the field and contribute. And indeed, reinforcement learning instantly solved all the locomotion problems. At the same time, in the future you can see that prompt engineering is something almost anyone can do because it is natural language. You can interact with the model in various ways to make it help you do things. After I reached that later stage, I realized that reinforcement learning had become widespread. When people in both the United States and China had begun using reinforcement learning to solve robot-gait problems, I felt I should perhaps move on to solve a harder problem, one that was not yet something everyone could solve.

items.question: How do you view Google’s shift from loosely organized research to large, coordinated teams?

Because everyone was very loosely organized, it was also hard for me to gather a group of people to do something big together. Gradually, I think Google realized this too: we do not want to be just an academic lab but very costly. items.question: How do you approach overcoming big-company bureaucracy to keep robotics research moving quickly at Google DeepMind?
items.object: Big-company bureaucracy and research iteration speed at Google DeepMind
items.answer: Big-company disease definitely exists. Big companies always need to obtain approval layer by layer for decisions. They are very conservative in many areas. Big companies always have all kinds of monopoly and PR risks, so I think big companies overall are relatively conservative. Besides doing research, I also have another responsibility to the team called research iteration speed. That means I have to ensure that things people want to do can be done quickly. But that means fighting the whole big-company disease. If a researcher says they want to use certain data, but the company says, to use this data I need due diligence, legal compliance, this review and that review, then the process is very complicated. It may take several weeks, and you cannot use the data at all. Or if I want to try a new robot, Google used to take perhaps more than 30 business days from expressing that intent to being able to issue the purchase order. That is all extremely slow. I have had to work extensively with many internal Google teams, such as legal teams, or operations teams, to tell them that in this era, you cannot afford to wait. After 30 days, those researchers with a strong sense of mission will all have left. This era truly cannot wait, or someone else will already have built it. So I think that, from the top down, Google DeepMind attaches great importance to robotics. They have opened many special cases so we can accelerate iteration speed in every area, whether procurement, experiments, data, and so on. What I mean is: big-company disease still exists, but if your work is in a very important and highly competitive area, I think you still have some leverage to make the company change things for your team.

items.question: How do you understand Meta's impact on the price of AI talent in Silicon Valley?
items.object: Meta's impact on AI talent prices in Silicon Valley
items.answer: The change has been huge. I think Meta has done several things. First, it has driven up the price of AI talent to a very high level. I do not actually know whether AI talent is really worth that much money. There are several explanations. The first is that it is caused by supply and demand: all big companies want to develop AI and be AI-first, so demand is huge. But the supply of AI talent, especially the highest-quality AI talent, is very limited. The supply-demand relationship has made the price very high—that is one explanation. The second is that AI talent really is worth that price because compute is extremely expensive. If you waste compute, that is also a huge amount of money. Better to spend money hiring people to use that compute well and create value, because the value is much greater than those people's cost. That is the second explanation: the value is there. A third explanation is that poaching these people is still cheaper than acquiring similar companies to acquire the people. So the price is still worth it. I do not know—it is hard to judge whether one person is worth USD 100 million—but I think Meta's recent series of moves has indeed disrupted the entire Silicon Valley price for AI talent.

items.question: How do you think robotics will progress toward truly general capabilities?

Their hardware is very capable, but they have no brain; still, you can make them do many things by teleoperation. You can basically see this now. For example, Tesla uses teleoperation in many scenarios, but sometimes you cannot tell whether it is teleoperated or autonomous. That shows the robot hardware is already very mature. items.question: How do you compare the way children learn and develop with the way robots do?
items.object: The similarities between children's learning and robot development
items.answer: They are very similar. Children basically learn in two ways. One is reinforcement learning. They constantly explore, receive a certain reward, and reinforce their ability to do things. The second is imitation: they watch what their parents do, watch what their peers around them do, and slowly learn. These two are very similar. I often make analogies, saying, “Our robot is like two years old.” You can feel that as a child develops, they gradually acquire vision; after they have vision, they gradually learn to grasp, to pick things up. Then they can gradually sit up and begin walking—locomotion. Many things are very similar to AI development. It is just that manipulation happens earlier for kids, but for robots, manipulation is way harder than locomotion.

items.question: How do you assess expectations about how soon robots will be ready for real-world use?
items.object: Public expectations of robotics development and deployment
items.answer: I think the vast majority of people, especially those outside the robotics industry, overestimate robotics development. People are used to taking out the best result and filming a video, even though that video is not very representative. It may only represent the best result out of ten takes. But when viewers see the video, they think that is the capability the robot already has. So people may think that next year they will be able to buy a humanoid robot to serve them at home. I think investors may be a little more clear-eyed, but investors also often overestimate the development of the industry as a whole. So what I want to say is: personally, although I feel very excited and think this is a very good moment and era, we still need to stay calm and truly understand the current state of robots. Although technological development overall is accelerating, the gap to robot applications is still fairly large. So we still need to wait for a while for robots to truly be deployed.

items.question: How do you judge whether the robotics industry is in a huge bubble?
items.object: A potential bubble in the robotics industry
items.answer: It may have a huge bubble. That depends first on how quickly robots develop, because perhaps they will continue accelerating over the next two years. Second, it depends on whether people find deployment scenarios, just as people have started looking for them. A year ago, I thought it was impossible for this kind of AI robot to be deployed in the short term. But now people seem to have found some directions that may be deployable. If this pace continues to accelerate and deployment continues happening, then perhaps it is not a bubble.
